fieldsRead.programmeDescription: Art History at Radboud studies artworks, architecture and visual culture in their historical contexts, from antiquity to the present. It combines visual analysis, art-historical theories and methods, museum visits and independent research.
fieldsRead.comparisonExplanation: A complete UCR comparison is withheld while Radboud’s current curriculum needs clarification. The same Paris course appears in two years, leaving 10 EC without a verified distinct allocation. Art history, heritage and visual-media connections at UCR remain promising, but they are not approved programmes here.

curriculum.limitation: The degree is 180 EC. This list accounts for 170 distinct EC because the same 10-EC Paris course appears in both year 2 and year 3. The remaining 10 EC need clarification. Future Florence and Kunstwerelden courses are not treated as current replacements. This is a partial list, not a complete degree pathway. Required first-year mentoring, the Dutch academic-language diagnostic and second-year personal/professional development add no credits. Attendance applies to mentoring and seminars.

componentNotes.y2-06: Restricted choice: two permitted 15-EC Faculty of Arts minors, one per semester, not a universal set of six named electives.
componentNotes.y3-02: One permitted 5 EC choice, selected from four alternatives and not previously counted in year 2. Other choices include Latin American art, classical reception and Low Countries art.
componentNotes.y3-03: Required 5 EC career and personal/professional development course. The current programme does not require the future Kunstwerelden course here.
componentNotes.y3-04: Required 10 EC independent art-history research with preparatory meetings, written agreement, supervisor and second reader. The current OER permits entry after Florence or Paris; the catalogue still states both.
componentNotes.y3-05: 30 EC bachelor-level broadening outside the student’s own programme. Optional internship/exchange must meet applicable approval and overlap rules.

preparedDescriptions.name: Personal & Professional Development
preparedDescriptions.text: This course is a first-year requirement and aims to stimulate personal development, namely, being able to actively, consciously and ethically orientate oneself in relation to others and the world. It supports the development of core personal and academic skills that enhance critical thinking and independent learning. It seeks to improve and develop academic writing and presenting skills and helps students develop the foundational skills and attitudes to reflect on societal issues and engage with societal partners.

provenance.reviewNote: CP256: read the selected text and current course evidence in full. The concise cached description makes supported subject/method claims, with no unsupported disciplinary or project guarantee. Displayed text retained unchanged; source provenance recorded.

preparedDescriptions.name: Building with Nature
preparedDescriptions.text: Introduces the sustainable engineering approach of working with natural processes for flood protection, land reclamation and port development. Covers history and principles of ecosystem‑based design, explores case studies and includes guest lectures and field excursions.

provenance.reviewNote: CP077: complete selected official description read against current course evidence. Retain accurate overview without extra methods, depth or equivalence inferred.

preparedDescriptions.name: Living with Water
preparedDescriptions.text: Studies water risks and opportunities in deltas, using Zeeland as a central case. Flooding, freshwater scarcity, salinisation, subsidence and pollution are connected to infrastructure, history, governance, law and justice. Students evaluate engineered and nature-based responses, then apply these ideas through site-based inquiry and a project on delta adaptation.

provenance.reviewNote: Compared with the current selected workbook field. Revised the description to retain supported academic scope and activities without superseded or unsupported details.

preparedDescriptions.name: Governance of Sustainability
preparedDescriptions.text: This course examines sustainability through the lens of governance: “a process of rule-making and collective decision-making that includes both governmental and non-governmental actors in shaping public policy” (Fenger & Bekkers, 2016). Taking this lens, we ask questions such as how are sustainability policies on the local, national, and international level made and enforced? Which actors represent which interests, and which are most influential? How is public opinion on sustainability shaped, and how does public opinion shape politics? What, at the end of the day, determines effective policy for sustainability? By the end of this course, you will have gained a deep appreciation of the complexity of the governance dimension of sustainability, and have developed the theoretical and practical understanding to critically assess mainstream policy decisions.

provenance.reviewNote: CP256: read the selected text and current course evidence in full. The concise cached description makes supported subject/method claims, with no unsupported disciplinary or project guarantee. Displayed text retained unchanged; source provenance recorded.

preparedDescriptions.name: Climate Change
preparedDescriptions.text: Focuses on drivers and impacts of anthropogenic climate change on sea level, ocean acidification, ecology and society. Discusses adaptation and mitigation solutions, including renewable energy systems, carbon storage and climate‑adaptive planning, and examines climate governance and justice.

provenance.reviewNote: CP256: read the selected text and current course evidence in full. The concise cached description makes supported subject/method claims, with no unsupported disciplinary or project guarantee. Displayed text retained unchanged; source provenance recorded.

preparedDescriptions.name: Life Cycle Analysis & Circular Economy
preparedDescriptions.text: Teaches evaluation of environmental impacts of products, processes and services throughout their lifecycle. Emphasises strategic planning for a circular economy through hands‑on learning.

provenance.reviewNote: CP256: read the selected text and current course evidence in full. The concise cached description makes supported subject/method claims, with no unsupported disciplinary or project guarantee. Displayed text retained unchanged; source provenance recorded.

preparedDescriptions.name: Modern History
preparedDescriptions.text: Provides a chronological overview of history from 1815 to the present. Discusses industrialisation, popular sovereignty and national self‑determination, and covers major economic, political and cultural developments including revolutions, world wars and the fall of communism.

preparedDescriptions.name: History of Empires
preparedDescriptions.text: History of Empires examines empires across global history and competing theories of empire. Students study expansion, administration, military and economic systems, legitimacy, ideology, culture, decline and legacies. Historical cases, source analysis and an independent research essay connect theoretical interpretation with specific imperial experiences.

provenance.reviewNote: Compared with the current selected workbook field. Revised the description to retain supported academic scope and activities without superseded or unsupported details.

preparedDescriptions.name: Native American Histories
preparedDescriptions.text: Native American Histories studies Indigenous social and cultural histories from the nineteenth century to the present. Boarding schools, institutional violence, family separation and intergenerational trauma are connected to resistance, resurgence, food sovereignty and cultural expression. Storytelling, reciprocity and relational accountability guide collaboration with Indigenous peers and knowledge holders through arts-based work and a public-history project.

Students study utilitarianism, Kantian ethics, virtue ethics, contractarianism and feminist ethics, alongside Nietzsche, Murdoch and Nagel. Reflection and research essays develop interpretation, argument evaluation and an independent position on ethical theory or a practical ethical problem.

Students study views of human nature, society, rights and authority in historical context and compare their arguments with current political problems. Original texts, an essay and a group project develop interpretation and normative argument.

Structural inequality, identity and colonial legacies connect to international security, humanitarian law, human rights, peacebuilding and transitional justice. An interdisciplinary podcast, policy brief and research dossier develop analysis, while reflection examines how assumptions shape inquiry.

Topics include trust, social capital, public spheres, solidarity, social movements and civil repair. An experience report connects engagement or observation to course concepts, while an individual project uses theoretical and empirical sources to analyse a civil-society organisation, movement or initiative.

preparedDescriptions.text: Introduction to Western Art History surveys Western art from late-medieval and Renaissance painting to contemporary practice. Students relate artists, styles and movements to social, religious, political and cultural change. Close examination of paintings develops visual analysis, while a term paper combines study of a painting on location with art-historical evidence.

preparedDescriptions.text: Introduction to World Archaeology explores craft production and material culture in ancient societies around the world. Students examine how making objects relates to religious, social and gendered identities, technologies and environmental effects. An experimental educational activity and discussion of contemporary archaeological methods connect interpretation with practice.

preparedDescriptions.name: Renaissance Italy & Global Mediterranean
preparedDescriptions.text: This course examines the painting, sculpture, and architecture of Renaissance Italy and the extensive artistic connections that linked the Italian peninsula to other regions of the world. By exploring a range of geographical contexts, from the Islamic courts of the Eastern Mediterranean and the commercial routes connecting Europe, Asia, and Africa to the newly encountered territories of the Americas, students will examine how trade, colonization, and cross-cultural exchange shaped the production and meaning of Renaissance art.

preparedDescriptions.name: Greek Archaeology
preparedDescriptions.text: The invention of democracy in classical Greece changed the nature of community decision-making, perhaps forever. This process is reflected in the material culture of the period. By examining the archaeology of community & democracy in early-democratic Greece, this course goes in search of ancient lessons for the modern world.

preparedDescriptions.name: Heritage & Ancient Democracy
preparedDescriptions.text:
In the modern world democracy is associated with participation, rationality and freedom. In this course, we go back to the roots of democracy in ancient Greece, when to a modern observer, it was not very democratic at all: foreigners, slaves and women were excluded from elections and political decision-making. Even so, the inclusion of all classes, also the poor, in politics was after antiquity not achieved until the mid-nineteenth century.


Ancient commentators criticised Athenian democracy for being too extreme just because of this broad inclusion. They argued that many were too uneducated, too emotional, and too irrational to see through the cheap play on emotions by demagogues and would-be tyrants.


This course investigates how Athenian democracy was built, how it was intertwined with myth and religion, and expressed in art, literature and architecture. It traces the loci of democracy in archaeology, and analyses its temporary collapse in the crisis of the late fifth century BC. Most importantly, we put ourselves in our socio-political ancestors’ shoes by engaging in a simulation of the Athenian assembly, in which we have to make decisions that will change our lives forever. In doing so, we use the ancient heritage of democracy for an experiment in applied sociology – to not only understand, but to feel the meaning of political decision-making.

provenance.reviewNote: Compared with the current selected workbook field. Retained the existing description as a faithful account; updated its source provenance.

preparedDescriptions.name: Writing Art's Histories
preparedDescriptions.text: This course examines the history of art history as an academic discipline, tracing how scholars have understood and interpreted art from the sixteenth century to the present. Through critical readings of influential texts by figures such as Aby Warburg, Erwin Panofsky, Ernst Gombrich, Michel Foucault, and Jacques Derrida, students explore the major ideas and methodologies that have shaped the field. Topics include art and history, aesthetics, meaning and interpretation, authorship and identity, and the challenges of art history in a globalized world.

provenance.reviewNote: Compared with the current selected workbook field. Retained the existing description as a faithful account; updated its source provenance.

preparedDescriptions.name: Introduction to Literary Studies
preparedDescriptions.text: Introduction to Literary Studies introduces practical criticism and literary interpretation. Students examine what literature is, why it is read and studied, formal properties and the constructed character of texts. Fiction, poetry and drama are supplemented by contemporary nonfiction and basic film narration, developing critical terms, tools and techniques.

preparedDescriptions.name: World Myth & Literature
preparedDescriptions.text: World Myth & Literature compares mythic narratives across ancient and later traditions, examining transmission, cultural connections and themes such as creation, power, gender, love and loyalty. Greek, Roman, Near Eastern, Indian, Arabic and African materials support literary analysis. A research paper, graphic explanation and creative retelling connect interpretation with narrative practice.

preparedDescriptions.name: Introduction to Film & Media
preparedDescriptions.text: Introduction to Film & Media examines how moving images create meaning through cinematography, editing, sound, narrative and performance. Film history connects early cinema and major movements with feminist and postcolonial interpretation, alongside television, digital platforms and spectatorship. An analytical or creative-analytical project combines close analysis, theory and scholarly research.
